detail.design: Prospective cohort methodological analysis.
detail.aim: Test whether spot-urine sodium formulas produce outcome associations independent of measured sodium.
detail.methods: Analysed435,336 UK Biobank participants using three equations; repeated analyses after replacing urine sodium concentration with sex-specific constants.

detail.design: Secondary validation analysis of PURE China urine data.
detail.aim: Test morning fasting spot estimates of usual salt intake.

detail.design: Repeated national cross-sectional urine-survey comparison.
detail.aim: Test spot sodium for monitoring population salt-change trends.
detail.objectives: Compare direct spot concentration and estimating formulas with 24-hour excretion.
detail.methods: England adult surveys 2006–2014 supplied 2020 complete 24-hour and 21711 spot samples; sodium measures were compared across calendar time.
detail.statistics: Regression of measure on time, method and interaction; comparison of annual slopes.
detail.tools: Kawasaki, Tanaka and INTERSALT equations.
detail.findings: Measured daily salt declined 12%; spot concentration declined 13%, with parallel slopes. Formula estimates detected approximately no change.
detail.conclusions: Random representative spot concentrations may monitor relative population trends between full surveys.
detail.limitations: Population trend monitoring does not validate estimating an individual’s usual intake from a spot sample.

detail.design: Individual-participant analysis of six prospective cohorts.
detail.aim: Assess usual sodium/potassium exposure and cardiovascular risk.
detail.objectives: Estimate dose-response associations using repeat urine measures.
detail.methods: 10709 generally healthy adults supplied at least two 24-hour urines; 571 cardiovascular events occurred over median 8.8 years. Cohorts used consistent confounder-controlled analyses.
detail.statistics: Cohort analyses combined with random-effects meta-analysis.
detail.tools: Repeated 24-hour urinary sodium/potassium measurements.

detail.conclusions: Results support lower sodium and higher potassium intake.
detail.limitations: Prospective observational associations remain distinct from intervention effects despite repeat biomarker measurement.

nodes.citation: Naser AM, He FJ, Rahman M, Campbell NRC ( 2021 ) . Spot Urine Formulas to Estimate 24-Hour Urinary Sodium Excretion Alter the Dietary Sodium and Blood Pressure Relationship . Hypertension 2127 - 2137 .

detail.design: Pooled cohort methodological analysis.
detail.aim: Assess how sodium-estimation formulas alter sodium–blood-pressure associations.
detail.methods: Pooled 10,034 person-visits from three Bangladeshi cohorts with measured 24-hour urine electrolytes and blood pressure; substituted measured values and sex-specific sodium constants into three formulas.
detail.statistics: Bland–Altman analysis; adjusted multilevel linear models with restricted cubic splines.
detail.tools: Kawasaki, Tanaka and INTERSALT equations; 24-hour urine.
detail.findings: All formulas overestimated low sodium excretion and underestimated high excretion. Measured sodium had a linear systolic association; estimated sodium produced J-shaped associations even with constant sodium.
detail.conclusions: Intrinsic formula components can distort associations; these equations should not be used to study individual sodium–blood-pressure relationships.
detail.limitations: Pooled observational data; substituted 24-hour rather than spot concentrations tests equation structure, not actual spot-sampling performance.
objectives: Assess how sodium-estimation formulas alter sodium–blood-pressure associations.

detail.design: Cross-sectional SONIC study of Australian schoolchildren aged4–12 years.
detail.aim: Assess sodium intake associations with BMI z score, overweight/obesity and abdominal obesity.
detail.objectives: Assess sodium intake associations with BMI z score, overweight/obesity and abdominal obesity.
detail.methods: Convenience sample from 56schools;666children provided valid24-hour urine. Anthropometry used CDC BMI z scores, IOTF categories and waist:height ratio≥0.5. Dietary24-hour recall analysed in458children aged8–12.
detail.statistics: Multiple linear and logistic regression adjusted for age, sex and socioeconomic status, with school-clustered robust standard errors. Additional energy, sugar-sweetened beverage and BMI adjustment models; residual/linearity checks.
detail.tools: Stata/SE13.0; Siemens Advia2400; urinary ion-selective electrodes; Jaffe creatinine;24-hour dietary recall.
detail.findings: Per17 mmol/day higher urinary sodium (1 g/day salt), adjusted BMI z score difference0.10 (95%CI 0.07–0.13), overweight/obesity OR 1.23 (1.16–1.31), and abdominal-obesity OR 1.15 (1.09–1.23). Energy adjustment did not markedly change older-child associations; abdominal-obesity association did not persist after BMI adjustment.
detail.conclusions: Higher urinary sodium was associated with adiposity; longitudinal studies are needed to evaluate causality.
detail.limitations: Cross-sectional design, convenience recruitment and low response; no dietary data for younger children; dietary recall and urine were not concurrent, and energy measurement error may remain.

nodes.methods: DerSimonian-Laird random effects; I-squared; Egger/funnel; meta-regression; correlation sensitivity 0.1–0.9
nodes.citation: Huang L, Trieu K, Yoshimura S, Neal B, Woodward M, Campbell NRC, Li Q, Lackland. DT et al. ( 2020 ) . Effect of Dose and Duration of Dietary Sodium Reduction on Blood Pressure Levels: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomised Trials . BMJ: British Medical Journal

detail.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised sodium-reduction trials.
detail.aim: Examine the dose-response relationship between sodium reduction and blood-pressure change and the influence of intervention duration.
detail.objectives: Pool sodium and blood-pressure effects; investigate dose, duration, and sources of heterogeneity.
detail.methods: Searched MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, and reference lists through January 2019. Eligible adult trials assessed sodium using 24-hour urinary excretion. Screening and extraction included independent checking.
detail.statistics: DerSimonian–Laird random-effects pooling; subgroup analyses; meta-regression; I²; funnel plots and Egger testing. Sensitivity analyses varied assumed paired correlations from 0.1 to 0.9.
detail.tools: Stata 15.1.
detail.findings: Across 133 studies involving 12,197 participants, sodium reduction lowered systolic and diastolic blood pressure.
detail.conclusions: Randomised evidence supports blood-pressure reduction through lower sodium intake.
detail.limitations: Trial duration, sodium reduction, populations, and outcome variances differed; some paired variances required assumptions.

detail.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
detail.aim: Examine sodium intake, adiposity and sweetened-beverage consumption.
detail.methods: Included cross-sectional, longitudinal and randomised studies; intervention trials required at least three months. Pooled outcomes represented by at least three studies.
detail.statistics: Meta-analysis and energy-adjusted sensitivity analyses.

nodes.citation: Tan M, He FJ, Wang C, MacGregor GA ( 2019 ) . Twenty‐Four‐Hour Urinary Sodium and Potassium Excretion in China: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis . Journal of the American Heart Association vol. 8 , ( 14 )

detail.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
detail.aim: Estimate sodium and potassium intake in China from 24-hour urinary measurements.
detail.objectives: Compare age groups, regions and temporal patterns.
detail.methods: Searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, CNKI and Wanfang through February 2019; included Chinese 24-hour urinary studies, excluding hospitalised patients. Seventy studies supplied sodium data for 26767 participants;59 supplied potassium for 25564.
detail.statistics: Random-effects meta-analysis and meta-regression for heterogeneity.
detail.tools: 24-hour urinary sodium/potassium; five bibliographic databases.
detail.findings: Adults excreted 189.07 mmol sodium/day (95% CI 182.14–195.99) and 36.35 mmol potassium/day (35.11–37.59). Sodium was higher in northern China (P<0.0001), although declining there (P=0.0066).
detail.conclusions: High sodium and low potassium intakes support simultaneous sodium reduction and potassium improvement.
detail.limitations: Regional and temporal heterogeneity complicates a single national intake estimate; hospitalised populations were excluded.
detail.coverage: Primary manuscript abstract and available introduction/methods excerpts inspected.

nodes.citation: Doulton TWR, He FJ, MacGregor GA ( 2005 ) . Systematic Review of Combined Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibition and Angiotensin Receptor Blockade in Hypertension . Hypertension vol. 45 , ( 5 ) 880 - 886 .

detail.design: Meta-analysis of randomised trials.
detail.aim: Compare combined ACE-inhibitor/angiotensin-receptor blockade with either alone.
detail.methods: Searched MEDLINE, EMBASE and Cochrane for randomised comparisons of combined and single therapy.
detail.statistics: Meta-analysis with pooled blood-pressure differences and confidence intervals.
detail.tools: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers; ambulatory/clinic pressure.
detail.findings: Combination lowered ambulatory pressure by 4.7/3.0 mmHg versus ACE monotherapy and 3.8/2.9 versus receptor-blocker monotherapy; adequately dosed longer-acting ACE therapy often showed no added effect.
detail.conclusions: Authors did not recommend routine combination treatment for uncomplicated hypertension without better studies.
detail.limitations: Trials were insufficiently large/long to establish safety; dosing limitations complicated efficacy interpretation.
objectives: Compare combined ACE-inhibitor/angiotensin-receptor blockade with either alone.

detail.design: Meta-analysis of randomised modest salt-reduction trials.
detail.aim: Quantify blood-pressure effects of sustained modest salt reduction.
detail.methods: Searched MEDLINE/EMBASE/Cochrane/CINAHL and references; included trials at least four weeks: 17 hypertensive and 11 normotensive trials.
detail.statistics: Meta-analysis, meta-regression, funnel plots and weighted linear dose–response regression.
detail.tools: 24-hour urinary sodium; four bibliographic sources.
detail.findings: Pooled pressure falls were 4.96/2.73 mmHg in hypertensives and 2.03/0.97 in normotensives; sodium-change dose response was observed.
detail.conclusions: Modest reduction over at least four weeks lowers pressure in both groups.
detail.limitations: Clinical mortality changes are predicted rather than observed; abstract cannot establish complete risk-of-bias methods.
objectives: Quantify blood-pressure effects of sustained modest salt reduction.

detail.design: Umbrella-review preprint, version 1, not peer reviewed.
detail.aim: Assess efficacy, safety and review quality of potassium-containing lower-sodium salts.
detail.objectives: Assess efficacy, safety and review quality of potassium-containing lower-sodium salts.
detail.methods: PROSPEROCRD 420261294404;5 databases through 6 March 2026;11 reviews, graded 1 high/3 moderate/5 low/2 criticallylow confidence; overlap assessed.
detail.statistics: Corrected covered area 28.5%; review-level pooled effect ranges, not a newly pooled umbrella estimate; software not stated.
detail.tools: Pub Med, Embase, Web of Science, Global Health/EBSCO and Cochrane review database.

detail.design: Exploratory stakeholder survey and focus-group study.

nodes.citation: Action on Salt (2014). Salt in Children.

detail.design: Observational study of dietary salt intake and sources among children/adolescents; archive summary.
detail.aim: Assess children’s dietary salt sources.
objectives: Compare the reported measures across products, groups or applicable criteria.
detail.methods: Archive summary of the South London child/adolescent salt-intake study; detailed sampling and measurement methods are not provided on this page.
detail.statistics: Descriptive composition comparisons, counts and percentages; complete inferential methods not extracted.
tools: Statistical software not reported in inspected archive text.
detail.findings: Bread/cereals contributed 36% of salt, meat products 19%, dairy 11% and crisps/snacks 5%. Boys’ reported intake exceeded girls’ by about 1 g/day in ages 5–6 and 2.5 g/day in ages 13–17.
detail.conclusions: The researchers support reducing salt in manufactured foods and clearer labelling.
detail.limitations: The archive omits participant count and measurement procedures; clinical effects were discussed as background, not measured intervention outcomes.
detail.coverage: Official archive article inspected; linked full report/research article not fully extracted.

nodes.authors: Brinsden HC, He FJ, Jenner KH, Macgregor GA
nodes.title: Surveys of the salt content in UK bread: progress made and further reductions possible
nodes.publication_type: Institutional record; type awaiting publisher metadata
nodes.attribution: Official personal publication list; unit attribution not automatically established
nodes.citation: Brinsden HC, He FJ, Jenner KH, Macgregor GA ( 2013 ) . Surveys of the salt content in UK bread: progress made and further reductions possible . BMJ Open vol. 3 , ( 6 )

detail.design: Repeated cross-sectional bread surveys.
detail.aim: Examine UK bread salt reductions and remaining scope for reformulation.
detail.methods: Compared supermarket bread samples in2001,2006and2011; assessed salt per100g, targets, brands/types and18 products present throughout.
detail.statistics: Descriptive and matched-product comparisons; exact test unspecified in abstract.
detail.findings: Mean salt fell from 1.23to0.98 g/100g, approximately 20%; matched products showed17% reduction.
detail.conclusions: Progressive targets may support further reductions.
detail.limitations: Changing assortments and small matched sample affect comparability; labels and product availability do not quantify intake or establish the policy counterfactual.

detail.design: Two-arm cluster-randomised trial.
detail.aim: Assess a small-change lifestyle intervention among urban Ugandan women.
detail.methods: Six Kampala churches allocated women aged 18–45 with waist circumference ≥80cm to infographics plus group sessions or infographics alone. Intervention lasted three months, followed by three-month follow-up.
detail.statistics: Intention-to-treat linear mixed models.
tools: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04635332
detail.findings: At six months, estimated waist difference was −1.87cm (95% CI −3.32 to −0.44). Diet and activity improved, alongside limited cardiometabolic changes.
detail.conclusions: Sustained lifestyle changes may benefit metabolic health over longer periods.
detail.limitations: Only six clusters and short follow-up constrain generalisation and assessment of long-term disease effects.

nodes.citation: Zhang X, Zhang P, Shen D, Li Y, He FJ, Ma J, Yan W, Gao Y et al. ( 2023 ) . Effect of home cook interventions for salt reduction in China: cluster randomised controlled trial . The BMJ vol. 382 ,

detail.design: Cluster randomised controlled trial of home-cook interventions in China.
detail.aim: Evaluate an intervention targeting salt added during household cooking.
detail.objectives: Assess whether supporting home cooks reduces salt intake.
detail.methods: Sixty communities in six Chinese provinces were randomised. A 12-month package combined six education sessions, supportive environments and seven-day weighing of salt/condiments. Baseline included 1,576 adults from 788 families; 10% were lost to follow-up. Outcomes included 24-hour urinary sodium and blood pressure.
detail.statistics: Adjusted mixed linear models compared change between groups.
detail.tools: 24-hour urine collection; educational and practical support for home cooks.
detail.findings: Urinary sodium was lower by 336.8 mg/24 h (95% CI 127.9–545.7). Systolic and diastolic pressure were lower by 2.0 and 1.1 mm Hg, respectively.
detail.conclusions: The home-cook/family intervention reduced sodium intake and blood pressure in this setting.
detail.limitations: Ten percent attrition and the household-cooking setting affect interpretation and transferability. Broader programme outcomes require separate assessment.

detail.design: Parallel cluster randomised controlled trial in 48 towns across six Chinese provinces.
detail.aim: Determine whether a town-level comprehensive programme lowers population salt intake.
detail.objectives: Evaluate changes in 24-hour urinary sodium after one year of multicomponent intervention.
detail.methods: Participants aged 18–75 completed urine collections, anthropometric measurements, and questionnaires at baseline and follow-up. The intervention combined community education with activities involving schools, restaurants, and other local settings.
detail.statistics: The abstract reports an intervention-versus-control comparison of salt-intake change. Exact model and software were not recovered.
detail.tools: 24-hour urine collection; anthropometry; questionnaires; community educational materials.
detail.findings: The one-year comparison did not show a statistically significant intervention effect on mean salt intake.
detail.conclusions: The comprehensive programme did not demonstrate reduced mean salt intake at its one-year endpoint.
detail.limitations: This endpoint differs from subsequent scale-up and longer-term assessments; those reports should remain linked but separately interpreted.

detail.design: Parallel cluster randomised controlled trial of AppSalt in Chinese schoolchildren and their families.
detail.aim: Evaluate app-supported school education for reducing salt intake.
detail.objectives: Measure changes in salt intake and blood pressure in children and adult family members.
detail.methods: The intervention combined a mobile application with primary-school delivery and a child-to-parent approach. Salt intake was assessed using 24-hour urinary sodium.
detail.statistics: Cluster-trial effect estimation; exact analysis model and software were not recovered in this inspection.
detail.tools: AppSalt mobile application; school-based education; 24-hour urine collection; blood-pressure measurement.
detail.findings: The programme lowered salt intake and systolic blood pressure among adults. Effects in children were not statistically significant.
detail.conclusions: App-supported child-to-parent education can benefit adult household members, while effectiveness in children requires separate assessment.
detail.limitations: Adult findings cannot establish effectiveness in children. Intervention effects are specific to the programme and setting.

nodes.citation: Du W, Zhang P, Zhang J, Li Y, He FJ, Zhang X, Su C, Jia X et al. ( 2022 ) . Sodium Reduction in Restaurant Food: A Randomized Controlled Trial in China . Nutrients vol. 14 , ( 24 )

detail.design: Randomised controlled trial with restaurants as the intervention units in China.
detail.aim: Evaluate a restaurant intervention to reduce sodium in food.
detail.objectives: Compare changes in the sodium content of best-selling dishes and examine restaurant practices and customer salt-related knowledge.
detail.methods: Randomised 192 restaurants 1:1 to a year-long intervention or control. Sodium change was measured in five best-selling dishes per restaurant. Follow-up was completed by 80 intervention and 66 control restaurants.
detail.statistics: Between-group change adjusted for confounders; exact model specification requires full-text review.
detail.tools: Protocol tools include customised electronic data capture, dish weighing and photography, and flame atomic absorption spectrometry. Outcome-paper implementation details were not independently recovered.
detail.findings: Estimated sodium reduction was 43.63 mg/100 g (95% CI −5.66 to 92.94 for the reduction; P=0.08), about 8%. The interval included no effect.
detail.conclusions: A modest reduction was estimated, but the study did not establish a statistically significant intervention effect.
detail.limitations: Substantial restaurant attrition and a dish-level outcome constrain inference; daily individual intake was not measured.

detail.design: Parallel randomised controlled trial; conference abstract.
detail.aim: Test salt reduction effects on pressure in stable kidney-transplant recipients.
detail.methods: Randomised 60 recipients at least six months post-transplant to 150 versus 80 mmol/day sodium targets for eight weeks; assessed 48-hour urinary sodium and pressure.
detail.statistics: Adjusted between-group mean differences with confidence intervals.
detail.tools: 48-hour urine; office and ambulatory pressure; proteinuria and eGFR.
detail.findings: Sodium fell by adjusted 36 mmol/day relative to control; office systolic difference was −2 mmHg (95% CI −12 to 9), with no significant pressure, proteinuria or eGFR effect.
detail.conclusions: A roughly 2 g/day salt reduction did not significantly lower office pressure in this sample.
detail.limitations: Small short trial with controlled baseline pressure and lower-than-expected sodium; wide pressure uncertainty.
objectives: Test salt reduction effects on pressure in stable kidney-transplant recipients.

detail.design: Molecular substudy of double-blind randomised crossover sodium trial.
detail.aim: Identify circulating miRNA responses to sodium reduction.
detail.objectives: Discover signals and validate associations with vascular phenotypes.
detail.methods: RNA sequencing used paired samples from 10 untreated Black male hypertensives; validation assessed all 64 Black hypertensive participants using paired intervention-period samples.
detail.tools: Whole-genome RNA sequencing; PCR Serum/Plasma Focus panel.
detail.findings: Fifteen discovery miRNAs responded; miR-143-3 p replicated. Its increase accompanied reduced BP/arterial stiffness and increased skin capillary density.

detail.design: Three-arm pilot feasibility cluster randomised trial; preprint version 1, not peer reviewed.
detail.aim: Assess feasibility of community-facilitator participatory learning/action infant-feeding groups.
detail.objectives: Test prespecified recruitment/attendance/retention criteria and exploratory feeding/BMI outcomes.
detail.methods: 12 East London wards randomised 1:1:1 to face-to-face PLA, online PLA or usualcare, May–September 2022;8 biweekly sessions over 14 weeks.
detail.statistics: Prespecified Go/Stop criteria; exploratory baseline/follow-up comparisons; exact models/software not stated.
detail.tools: CEBQ; PFSQ; child BMIZscore; multilingual community facilitators; ISRCTN10234623.
detail.findings: 263 enrolled,261 recordedallocation; consent 186/263(70.7%,95%CI 65.0–75.9)met≥50%Go. Attendance 37%failed≥80%threshold; retention 54.8%triggered Stop. No group completed PLAphases 3/4. CEBQ/PFSQ lacked usable follow-up; baselineimbalances included BMI(P 0.005); follow-up BMIcomparison P 0.249.
detail.conclusions: Recruitment/acceptability supported, but retention/phase-completion/data problems prevent definitive outcome evaluation.
detail.limitations: Pilot scope and incomplete outcomes; abstract reports retention CI 41.8–55.3%alongside 54.8%point estimate and differing borough counts; these values are retained as reported, not reconciled from unread full text. P 0.249 does not establish equivalence.

Estimated Dietary and Health Impact of the World Health Organization’s Global Sodium Benchmarks on Packaged Foods in Australia: a Modeling Study . Hypertension vol. 80 , ( 3 ) 541 - 549 .

detail.design: Comparative risk-assessment modelling study.
detail.aim: Estimate Australian dietary and health effects of WHO packaged-food sodium benchmarks.
detail.methods: Combined representative food/sodium intake, product composition and sales data for 24 age–sex groups; compared full WHO compliance with Australian 2020 targets.
detail.statistics: Comparative risk assessment with uncertainty intervals.
detail.tools: National dietary and food-sales data; WHO and Australian benchmarks.
detail.findings: WHO compliance was modelled to reduce adult sodium by 404 mg/day (12%), avert 1,770 deaths/year (95% UI 1,168–2,587), 6,900 incident cases and 25,700 DALYs; estimated deaths averted exceeded Australian targets about 3.5-fold.
detail.conclusions: Adopting broader, tighter WHO benchmarks could yield greater health gains.
detail.limitations: Modelled full compliance is a scenario; results do not establish achieved reformulation or observed health effects.
objectives: Estimate Australian dietary and health effects of WHO packaged-food sodium benchmarks.

detail.design: Retrospective interrupted time-series natural experiment.
detail.aim: Assess grocery-store placement and fruit/vegetable purchasing on Warwick campus.
detail.objectives: Assess grocery-store placement and fruit/vegetable purchasing on Warwick campus.
detail.methods: Daily 2012–2017 sales aggregated to 170 term-timeweeks:90 baseline,40 after January 2015 prominent produce placement,40 after April 2016 displayreplacement. Outcomes were produce share by quantity/money.
detail.statistics: Dynamic multiple regression with ARIMAerrors, time and final-term-week covariates; auto.arima model selection; ANOVA; Ljung–Box residual tests and VIF checks.
detail.tools: R; xts, ggplot 2, forecast/auto.arima.
detail.findings: Prominent placement associated with 0.97 percentage-point quantity-share and 0.69 point money-share increases against declining time trend. Replacement display coefficient positive but not statistically significant. Ljung–Box residual tests were significant; authors found no concerning visible autocorrelation pattern.
detail.conclusions: Placement may support healthier purchasing; declining produce share warrants investigation.
detail.limitations: One uncontrolled store; first change accompanied renovation/branding, purchases are not intake, price/pack-size alternatives exist. Exact coefficient CIs/tables not inspected; residual tests remain a modelling limitation.

detail.design: Trial-based economic evaluation with Markov modelling.

sources.abstract_text: Over half of urban populations in Sub-Saharan Africa live in deprived urban neighbourhoods, where individuals have a high risk of TB and often unfavourable outcomes. We summarise key insights from recent workshops held in Freetown (Sierra Leone) and Maputo (Mozambique), emphasising an urgent need for more coherent TB control. Encouragingly, ad-hoc solutions are being piloted in these settings, focussing on targeted TB screening with portable and accessible tests. Amid a decline in aid funding, we argue that a more focused approach to targeting TB hotspots, leveraging affordable mobile technology, is essential.

sources.abstract_text: Strong evidence indicates that reduction of salt intake lowers blood pressure and reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD). The WHO has set a global target of reducing the population salt intake from the current level of approximately 10 g daily to <5 g daily. This recommendation has been challenged by several studies, including cohort studies, which have suggested a J-shaped relationship between salt intake and CVD risk. However, these studies had severe methodological problems, such as reverse causality and measurement error due to assessment of salt intake by spot urine. Consequently, findings from such studies should not be used to derail vital public health policy. Gradual, stepwise salt reduction as recommended by the WHO remains an achievable, affordable, effective, and important strategy to prevent CVD worldwide. The question now is how to reduce population salt intake. In most developed countries, salt reduction can be achieved by a gradual and sustained reduction in the amount of salt added to food by the food industry. The UK has pioneered a successful salt-reduction programme by setting incremental targets for >85 categories of food; many other developed countries are following the UK's lead. In developing countries where most of the salt is added by consumers, public health campaigns have a major role. Every country should adopt a coherent, workable strategy. Even a modest reduction in salt intake across the whole population can lead to a major improvement in public health and cost savings.

detail.design: Cross-sectional South London child/adolescent dietary survey.
detail.aim: Estimate24-hour urinary salt intake and dietary sources against age-specific recommendations.
detail.objectives: Estimate24-hour urinary salt intake and dietary sources against age-specific recommendations.
detail.methods: 340valid24-hour urine collections in ages5–6,8–9,13–17;24-hour photographic food diaries. Recruited mainly from schools in Wandsworth/Sutton/Merton plus university spring school, October2007–June2010.
detail.statistics: Means and95%CIs by age tier and proportions above derived recommendations; exact comparative model/software not inspected.
detail.tools: 24-hour urine; ion-selective sodium/potassium electrodes; Jaffe then enzymatic creatinine assays; photographic food diary.
detail.findings: Mean salt3.75g/day (95%CI3.49–4.01),4.72 (4.33–5.11),7.55 (6.88–8.22) respectively;66%,73%,73%above recommendations. Cereals/cereal products supplied36% (bread15%), meat19%, milk products11%of dietary salt.
detail.conclusions: High intake and processed-food contributions support further manufactured-food salt reduction.
detail.limitations: Local cross-sectional sample; urine incompleteness screened using timing, missed voids, creatinine and volume. Derived age recommendations and single-day measurement limit interpretation of individual usual intake.

nodes.citation: Pombo-Rodrigues S, Calame W ( 2011 ) . The effects of consuming eggs for lunch on satiety and subsequent food intake . International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition vol. 62 , ( 6 ) 593 - 599 .

detail.design: Randomised three-way crossover feeding study.
detail.aim: Compare egg lunch with alternative lunches on satiety and subsequent energy intake.
detail.objectives: Compare egg lunch with alternative lunches on satiety and subsequent energy intake.
detail.methods: 31healthy men/women consumed standard breakfast then isocaloric omelette, jacket-potato or chicken-sandwich lunches; visual-analogue satiety recorded through day; ad-libitum meal after4hours measured energy intake.
detail.statistics: Abstract reports stronger satiety versus potato and no detected energy-intake effect; exact estimates/tests/software not stated.
detail.tools: Visual analogue scales; isocaloric meals; ad-libitum meal.
detail.findings: Omelette produced significantly stronger satiating response than jacket potato; no energy-intake effect was detected.
detail.conclusions: Egg-based lunch may increase perceived satiety compared with carbohydrate-based lunch; reduced subsequent energy intake was not demonstrated.
detail.limitations: Small acute feeding study; abstract lacks effect estimates, uncertainty, washout and sequence details; cannot establish long-term weight effects.
detail.coverage: Institutional dc.description.abstract field only; full text not inspected.

sources.abstract_text: The aim of the present work was to investigate the effects of eggs consumed for lunch on satiety, satiation and subsequent energy intake at the next meal. Thirty-one healthy male and female subjects participated in a randomized, three-way, crossover study. Following consumption of a standard breakfast, participants were asked to consume three isocaloric test lunches: omelette, jacket potato and chicken sandwich. Subjective measures of satiety were recorded using visual analog scales at regular intervals throughout the day. Energy intake at the next meal was assessed 4 h after lunch with an ad libitum meal. The egg lunch showed a significantly stronger satiating effect compared with the jacket potato meal. No effect on energy intake was seen. These data indicate that consumption of an omelette meal consumed at lunch could increase satiety to a greater extent than a carbohydrate meal and may facilitate reduction of energy consumption between meals.

detail.design: Reanalysis of controlled sodium-intake studies.
detail.aim: Assess plasma sodium changes with dietary salt changes.

detail.tools: Controlled sodium diets; plasma sodium; blood-pressure measures.

objectives: Assess plasma sodium changes with dietary salt changes.

detail.design: Trial meta-analysis with comparative dose–response and projected health impacts.
detail.aim: Assess how far population salt reduction could lower blood pressure.
detail.methods: Compared dose–response in longer-term trials with two controlled studies using three salt-intake levels; projected stroke and ischaemic-heart-disease effects.
detail.statistics: Meta-analytic dose–response and health-impact projections; exact model unspecified.
detail.tools: Trial data at salt intakes approximately 3–12 g/day.
detail.findings: A 3 g/day reduction predicted blood-pressure falls of 3.6–5.6/1.9–3.2 mmHg in hypertensives and 1.8–3.5/0.8–1.8 in normotensives. Stroke and heart-disease reductions were projections.
detail.conclusions: Authors propose 3 g/day as a longer-term population target.
detail.limitations: Projected clinical benefits are not observed events in these analyses; abstract does not detail selection or model assumptions.
objectives: Assess how far population salt reduction could lower blood pressure.

detail.design: Sequential short-term sodium restriction experiment.
detail.aim: Assess renin-system contributions to differential blood-pressure responses.
detail.methods: Ninety-three hypertensive and 39 normotensive White adults received about 350 mmol/day sodium for five days followed by 10–20 mmol/day for five days; measured pressure, renin and aldosterone.
detail.statistics: Age-adjusted group comparisons and correlations.
detail.tools: Controlled sodium diets; urinary sodium; plasma renin activity and aldosterone.
detail.findings: Hypertensives had an adjusted 7/7 mmHg greater pressure fall; renin and aldosterone rose less than in normotensives, with inverse correlations between hormonal rise and pressure fall.
detail.conclusions: Reduced renin-system responsiveness may partly explain larger pressure falls in hypertensives.
detail.limitations: Acute extreme sodium change and sequential order limit extrapolation to sustained modest restriction; random allocation not reported.
objectives: Assess renin-system contributions to differential blood-pressure responses.

detail.design: Multicentre dose-titration study with randomised double-blind placebo-controlled withdrawal phase.
detail.aim: Evaluate candesartan alone and with additional drugs in moderate-to-severe hypertension.
detail.methods: Recruited 216 patients; two-week placebo run-in, 12-week open-label escalation/addition of amlodipine/hydrochlorothiazide, then four-week randomised candesartan withdrawal.
detail.statistics: ANCOVA for withdrawal-phase treatment comparison.
detail.tools: Candesartan cilexetil, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide; sitting blood-pressure measurement.
detail.findings: Mean pressure fell from 175/108 to 141/88 mmHg during escalation; candesartan withdrawal in 67 placebo recipients increased pressure 13/6 mmHg relative to continuation (p<0.0001).
detail.conclusions: Candesartan was effective and well tolerated within this treatment sequence.
detail.limitations: Open-label escalation includes co-treatment; withdrawal comparison is short term and does not measure cardiovascular outcomes.
objectives: Evaluate candesartan alone and with additional drugs in moderate-to-severe hypertension.

detail.design: Cross-sectional dietary/environmental preprint, version 1.
detail.aim: Compare nutrient intake and greenhouse-gas emissions in omnivorous, vegetarian and vegan UK children.
detail.objectives: Compare nutrient intake and greenhouse-gas emissions in omnivorous, vegetarian and vegan UK children.
detail.methods: 39 children aged 2–12:15 omnivore,11 vegetarian,13 vegan;3-day weighed diaries; nutrients with/without supplements and ingredient-level kg CO 2 e/day.
detail.statistics: Diet-group emission comparison P<0.001; exact comparison model/software other than nutrient platform not stated.
detail.tools: Nutritics; weighed diaries; Eatwell Guide categories.
detail.findings: No group met all nutrient reference values. Vegan iodine remained inadequate with supplementation; vitamin D inadequate without supplements in all groups. Vegan mean emissions 46%below omnivore and 20%below vegetarian.

detail.limitations: Secondary analysis of stored samples from 64 participants; metabolite–phenotype associations do not identify mediation.

detail.design: Systematic review with narrative synthesis.

detail.design: Qualitative focus-group/interview study; preprint.
detail.aim: Explore acceptability of school-canteen choice architecture.
detail.methods: Three groups with 15 adolescents and eight staff/caterer interviews at one Coventry school/provider.
detail.statistics: Qualitative analysis; exact method not specified in abstract.
detail.tools: Focus groups and interviews.
detail.findings: Convenience, presentation and value drove choices; proximity/positioning strategies were acceptable. Concerns included behaviour, food waste and reduced canteen use.

detail.design: Preprint mixed-methods EduSaltS process evaluation.
detail.aim: Explore real-world implementation and determinants of school-based digital salt education.
detail.objectives: Assess reach, education, adoption and sustained delivery within RE-AIM.
detail.methods: Combined website monitoring for 54,435 pupils, before/after questionnaires, 23 individual interviews and eight focus groups; triangulated quantitative and thematic findings.

detail.design: Qualitative stakeholder study in Malaysia, February2026.
detail.aim: Explore awareness, barriers and strategies for uptake of lower-sodium salt substitutes.
detail.objectives: Explore awareness, barriers and strategies for uptake of lower-sodium salt substitutes.
detail.methods: 24stakeholders from ministries/agencies, civil societies and academic/research institutions;75%women, mean age45.3±5.8 years. Semi-structured focus groups adapted from a4Aframework; recordings transcribed verbatim.

detail.design: Qualitative stakeholder preprint; not peer reviewed.
detail.aim: Explore stakeholder views to improve adolescent weight-management programmes.
detail.objectives: Assess professional, commissioning and referral perspectives in the Hearty Lives programme context.
detail.methods: Purposive recruitment of 11 women involved in West Midlands programme delivery/referral/commissioning; May–August 2018. Three face-to-face interviews,7 telephone interviews and 1 written email response. Mean interview 52 minutes(range 36–74).
detail.statistics: Inductive qualitative content analysis; open coding, subcategory/category abstraction; memos and independent author audit.
detail.tools: NVivo 11; semi-structured interview guide informed by qualitative systematic review.
detail.findings: Three main categories: professional support, tailoring and intervention content. Stakeholders favoured experienced nonjudgemental professional/family/peer support, longer follow-up, practical education, psychological support, flexible individual/group/home delivery and technology.
detail.conclusions: Stakeholder views can inform programme design; improved retention or efficacy was not demonstrated.
detail.limitations: All participants were women and selected through one local programme; researcher knew some participants. Ten additional school nurses did not participate. Source interview accounting includes 1 written response; no measured intervention outcome.

detail.aim: Develop valid spatial sampling in difficult urban settings.

detail.methods: Stakeholder engagement negotiates access; remote satellite mapping, local ground-truthing and resident enumeration generate spatial frames. Spatially regulated sampling is proposed to ensure coverage.
detail.tools: Satellite imagery; tablets and open-source data-collection software.
